newsitem.title: USA: World Bank sees "Green Revolution" in arid regions.
newsitem.headline: World Bank sees "Green Revolution" in arid regions.

text.p: Farmers living in some of the world's most forbidding and remote regions are getting their own version of the "Green Revolution" that averted famine in Asia and Latin America a generation ago, a World Bank official said on Thursday.

"These are some of the poorest farmers in the world and some of the least attractive terrains," said World Bank vice president Ismail Serageldin, in describing the challenge scientists face in improving the food crops grown in arid and semi-arid regions.

One-fourth of the world's population, or 1.6 billion people, live in developing nations and regions with insufficient rainfall. The crops that feed its people are overlooked in most plant breeding programs. Harsh climate and poor soils make it difficult to boost output.

Nonetheless, scientists at two research centers that are part of the Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research are scoring successes in developing higher-yielding and hardier crops for dry regions, said CGIAR Chairman Serageldin.

Among successes are pigeonpeas that mature in 110 days instead of the usual 180 days, a barley variety that doubles yields, and an early-maturing sorghum that was stabilizing production in sub-Saharan Africa.

A cold-tolerant variety of chickpeas can be planted in winter, instead of spring, to take advantage of seasonal rains. In places like northwest Bangladesh, the new variety can be sown as a second crop in a year, following rice, and greatly expanding a farm's output.

Overall, work at the International Crops Research Institute for Semi-Arid Tropics, in Andhra Pradesh, India, has resulted in the release of 365 new varieties that improved crop output and dependability.

The International Center for Agricultural Research in Dry Areas, in Aleppo, Syria, has worked with scientists in arid nations to develop more than 230 varieties of barley, lentils, faba beans, wheat, chickpeas and legumes.

The strategy of researchers has been to shorten the growing season for crops, to dodge drought and allow more than one crop a year. They also try to improve dryland livestock, which graze on tracts unsuited for crops and provide a livelihood for 300 million people worldwide.

During a telephone interview from Cairo, Serageldin said higher-yielding and drought-tolerant varieties were boosting food production in eastern Africa. Output has risen sharply in Ethiopia, he said, with the advent of ag development efforts.

The Green Revolution of the 1960s and 1970s was built on higher-yielding wheat and rice varieties that responded to fertilizers and irrigation. The crops foiled predictions of famine in the 1970s in Asia and other fast-growing areas.

CGIAR is supported by 53 donors, including U.N. agencies, the World Bank, foundations and major nations, who pledged about $325 million for this year. For the most part, pledges have been honored and CGIAR's 16 centers, with a couple of exceptions, are in sound shape, said Serageldin, who was in Cairo for a finance committee meeting.
